extracted.intended_audience: reporters, journalism students, and newspaper writers (including cub reporters and city editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing newspaper news stories, paragraphs, sentences, and word choice with emphasis on accuracy, clarity, brevity, and reader impact. Covers structural, grammatical, stylistic, and editorial rules for print journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied sentence length
rubrics_metrics.description: The story tone is greatly affected by sentence length; avoid sentences that are immoderately long or markedly short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a happy medium with simple constructions and a tendency toward shorter sentences than in other kinds of writing. Twenty words make a good average sentence length. Avoid monotonous, choppy (bing-bing-bing) style and excessively long, heavy sentences; remember readers include the uneducated as well as literati, so make style fluent and easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation (brevity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A diffuse style is never forceful; the reporter must condense ideas into the smallest space possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow city editor's space instructions exactly (e.g., don't submit 600 words when 500 are called for). If allotted more space than needed, introduce additional substantive details rather than filler words. Mere words do not make a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test of a story: accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The two cares for the reporter in writing the body of the story are accuracy and interest; accuracy is worth most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy is attained by strict adherence to truth with proof if questioned. Interest comes from making statements clear, coherent, and forceful. There is no single method; the final test is the story's effect upon the reader—if it attains the desired result, methods may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph as a mark of punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The paragraph sets off larger divisions of the story like punctuation; its indention signals a pause and shift to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use paragraphing for clearness and emphasis; treat paragraphing with similar principles as story structure while recognizing its own conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph clearness
rubrics_metrics.description: A paragraph's first requirement is that it be clear; its relation to adjacent paragraphs must be evident at a glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transitional phrases, sentences, or relation words when necessary, but rely mainly on natural and close sequence of ideas to show relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of each paragraph should be emphasized because fast readers catch the first words and phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the most important details at the start of a paragraph. Avoid beginning paragraphs with dependent clauses or subconnections; do not start successive paragraphs with the same words or constructions. Ensure paragraph endings are well rounded even if less emphatic than openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph length
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be brief and 'brief-looking'; modern readers will not tolerate long paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-sentence paragraphs are frequent in leads; two- or three-sentence paragraphs are common. Limit paragraphs to about 140 words (approx. 20 lines); 8–10 lines is a good average. Avoid half-column paragraphs; whenever in doubt about making a new paragraph, make one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence requisites: accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The same laws of accuracy and interest that apply to stories apply to sentences; because sentences are briefer and analyzable, the rules are more rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentence must be grammatically correct (accuracy) and clear and forceful (interest). The reader judges only the story; faulty, ungrammatical, or weak sentences will lose readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar: main error categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Main grammatical violations in news writing fall under four heads: faulty reference, incorrect verb forms, failures in coordinating/subordinating sentence parts, and poor ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to these four categories and correct them to ensure accurate sentences; city editors correct these errors frequently in cub copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun reference (pronouns referring to ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure every pronoun refers to a particular word in the sentence and agrees in gender and number; avoid using pronouns to refer to a general idea not expressed by a specific word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear pronoun reference is a prolific source of obscurity in news writing; rephrase or supply explicit nouns when antecedents are vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of pronouns in number
rubrics_metrics.description: Make reference words agree in number with the noun they refer to; watch collective nouns, distributive pronouns, and multiple noun constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors occur after words like crowd, council, jury; with distributives like everyone; and when two or more nouns require disambiguation. Recast sentences to avoid mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pronouns with unclear antecedents buried in the sentence so that the pronoun seems to refer to an intervening word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous use of pronouns is a common clarity error; rewrite sentences so the antecedent is obvious (examples provided in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Split infinitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The split infinitive (placing an adverb between to and the verb) is a common error among cub reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not always wrong (sometimes the only clear form), as a rule avoid split infinitives. Use rephrasing when possible to preserve clarity and convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitive and participle time relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinitives and participles have no finite tense of their own; they express time relative to the main verb, which can cause inaccuracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions that imply unintended timing (e.g., 'had intended to have arrested' vs. 'had intended to arrest'). Prefer clearer phrasing like 'having gone' or 'after going' when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangling participles
rubrics_metrics.description: A participle must have a definite noun or pronoun in the sentence to modify; dangling participles create incorrect or ludicrous meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the participle's logical subject is explicit (e.g., 'Having arrived at the county jail, the mob forced open the door' rather than implying the door arrived).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs must agree in number with their subjects; collective nouns can be singular or plural but must remain consistent; watch qualifiers between subject and verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid agreeing verbs to predicates; be careful with correlative constructions, expletive 'there' constructions, and intervening qualifying phrases that can mislead agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor) to connect items of equal grammatical rank; do not use them to connect unequal forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'and who' that join incompatible grammatical elements (e.g., participle with pronoun clause). Ensure paired elements are of the same grammatical type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clauses unequal in thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid connecting clauses equal in grammatical form when their thought-value is unequal; place the principal idea in the independent clause and the lesser idea in a dependent clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the clause containing the main idea independent and subordinate the less important idea (examples: reorder 'We were to raid the hall precisely at midnight, and we set our watches' into a subordinate-first construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis (omission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipsis is the omission of a word or phrase necessary to meaning; it is good when the omitted word can be readily supplied from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ellipses that force the reader to guess or re-read. Use ellipsis for brevity only when context makes the omission immediately understandable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness in the sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences must be clear and not require re-reading; clearness is more important than force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid reading requires sentences that yield ideas with minimal effort. Rewrite sentences that are grammatically correct but confusing or convoluted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep grammatically connected phrases close
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep dependent or modifying phrases close to the words they modify to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misplaced modifiers (e.g., 'over the governor's veto' placed far from 'pass') cause readers to pause; reorganize sentence to place modifiers next to their heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlative conjunction placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each part of correlative conjunctions (either...or, neither...nor, whether...or, not only...but also) should come immediately before the word or phrase it modifies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place 'either' or 'neither' directly before the element it governs (example: 'The prisoner will be either hanged or sentenced to life imprisonment' rather than 'Either the prisoner will be hanged or...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of 'only' and 'alone'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Only' belongs immediately before the word or phrase it modifies; 'alone' comes immediately after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing 'only' between emphatic words or isolating it incorrectly; re-order sentences so modifiers sit next to their targets to prevent unintended meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetic expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Long parenthetic expressions within a sentence often hinder clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extended parentheses in news writing; prefer two short, terse sentences which are clearer and more effective than one long sentence containing a doubtful parenthetic phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifted subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting the subject within a sentence or between adjoining sentences weakens clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain the same subject when possible across sentences; do not shift subject unnecessarily within a sentence—recast sentences to maintain a clear and stable subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sentence should both convey its own meaning and clarify the meaning of preceding and succeeding sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct connectives (and, or, but, etc.) and place phrases so relations between sentences are clear; wrong connective choice can make statements ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that seem to lack unity often need improved coherence rather than wholesale rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the logical relation explicit (e.g., add phrases to show cause/effect or sequence) so the sentence hangs together; use subordinate clauses where needed to maintain unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence emphasis (form, position, proportion, repetition, delicacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis is gained by sentence form, position, proportion (length), repetition, and delicacy of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place most important ideas at the beginning or end of a sentence; transform clauses into independent clauses for emphasis; use brevity for emphasis; use repetition carefully; and cultivate delicacy of expression (originality, tact, restraint) to avoid triteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion for emphasis (brevity and active verbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis varies inversely with sentence length; shorter sentences are more emphatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense predication—use as few verbs as possible and prefer active voice. Omit words that do not alter or obscure sense; present facts with a minimum of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (use and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition can gain coherence and emphasis but can become a handicap if overused or a sign of lazy vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition judiciously to link ideas or emphasize a point; avoid repeating the same adjective or phrase excessively (illustrated by overuse of 'beautiful' in bridal copy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicacy of expression is originality, cleverness, restraint, tact, and simplicity that distinguishes a star reporter from a cub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hackneyed openings, affectation, indelicate personal allusions, and triteness. Strive for grace, nimbleness of wit, and tasteful phrasing; examples show florid, overwrought wedding descriptions to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of a good sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A good sentence must possess the two requisites: accuracy and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy requires correct grammar, definite antecedents for pronouns, verb consistency, proper coordination/subordination, and effective ellipsis. Interest requires clarity, force, close placement of related words, avoidance of long parentheses, steady subjects, well-placed important ideas, concision, and delicacy of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words: accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: For words, as for sentences and stories, the rule is the same—accuracy and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose exact nouns, verbs, and adjectives; search until the single word that best expresses the idea is found. Avoid looseness of thinking and inexact expression; precision in word choice prevents errors and preserves credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in word choice; list of commonly misused pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must distinguish keenly between commonly confused word pairs and avoid misusing them (e.g., above/over, last/latest, administered/dealt, less/fewer, affect/effect, like/as if, materially/largely, allude/refer, notice/observe, and/ to, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the provided list of word pairs and use the correct member for the intended meaning. The text presents an extended inventory of words frequently misused by careless reporters—consult and internalize the distinctions to avoid inexactness.
